# Combining 2D and 3D graphics

A three-dimensional panel often needs two-dimensional companions:
ordinary ggplot2 layers drawn inside it, flat projections of the data on
the floor and walls of the box, or a contour map and a profile next to
it. This article shows each of these, then arranges 3D panels with 2D
panels using a second package. Installation is covered in [Get
started](https://gillescolling.com/ggplot3d/articles/ggplot3d.md). The
composition sections also use
[patchwork](https://patchwork.data-imaginist.com), the package that
arranges several ggplot2 plots on one page.

``` r

library(ggplot2)
library(ggplot3d)
library(patchwork)
```

## Plain ggplot2 layers in a 3D panel

The data below trace a helix. `track` contains an angle `t`, the
positions `x` and `y` on a unit circle, and a height `z` that rises from
1 to 3 over two turns. The ends are labelled in a second table.

``` r

track <- data.frame(t = seq(0, 4 * pi, length.out = 80))
track$x <- cos(track$t)
track$y <- sin(track$t)
track$z <- 1 + track$t / (2 * pi)
ends <- track[c(1, nrow(track)), ]
ends$label <- c("start", "end")
```

[`geom_path()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/geom_path.html),
[`geom_point()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/geom_point.html)
and
[`geom_text()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/geom_text.html)
are the ggplot2 layers, used unchanged. Inside
[`coord_3d()`](https://gillescolling.com/ggplot3d/reference/coord_3d.md)
they read the z mapping and are placed and depth sorted like
[`geom_path_3d()`](https://gillescolling.com/ggplot3d/reference/geom_point_3d.md),
[`geom_point_3d()`](https://gillescolling.com/ggplot3d/reference/geom_point_3d.md)
and
[`geom_text_3d()`](https://gillescolling.com/ggplot3d/reference/geom_point_3d.md).

``` r

h <- ggplot(track, aes(x, y, z = z))
h + geom_path(colour = "#2E6F9E", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_point(data = ends, colour = "#B5342B", size = 3) +
  geom_text(aes(label = label), data = ends, nudge_x = 0.35, size = 5) +
  coord_3d()
```

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Registered ggplot2 layers include points, paths, lines, segments, text,
labels, polygons, rectangles, tiles and intervals. Contour and density
contours draw each line at the height of its level. Filled contours draw
horizontal bands at their level midpoints, as shown in [Terraced filled
contours](#terraced-filled-contours). A layer without a z mapping is
drawn at z = 0, and the z scale extends to include 0. Here the path is
drawn a second time with `inherit.aes = FALSE`, so it lies flat at
height 0 below the helix.

``` r

h + geom_path(colour = "#2E6F9E", linewidth = 0.8) +
  geom_path(aes(x, y), inherit.aes = FALSE, colour = "#5C6166",
            linewidth = 0.8) +
  coord_3d()
```

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## Projecting points onto the floor and walls

A position of `-Inf` or `Inf` places a mark on the matching face of the
box, as `Inf` places a mark on the panel edge in ggplot2. The cloud
below has 40 points whose height follows `x + y` with noise.

``` r

set.seed(1)
cloud <- data.frame(x = rnorm(40), y = rnorm(40))
cloud$z <- cloud$x + cloud$y + rnorm(40, sd = 0.5)
```

Mapping `z = -Inf` draws each point’s shadow on the floor, and a
dropline joins each point to it. Mapping `y = Inf` draws the projection
onto the back wall at the largest y, where the points show z against x.

``` r

k <- ggplot(cloud, aes(x, y, z = z))
k + geom_point_3d(aes(z = -Inf), colour = "#5C6166", size = 1.5) +
  geom_point_3d(aes(y = Inf), colour = "#9E5E0F", size = 1.5) +
  geom_dropline_3d(onto = "zmin", colour = "#5C6166") +
  geom_point_3d(size = 2.5) +
  coord_3d()
```

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Shadows and wall projections use the same x, y and z scales as the
points, so each projection lies on the box grid at the coordinates it
shares with its point. The scales are trained on the finite positions
only, so the box keeps the range of the data.

## A whole 2D plot on a wall

A projection shows the points; a 2D plot on the wall can show a summary
of them as well.
[`annotation_plot_3d()`](https://gillescolling.com/ggplot3d/reference/annotation_plot_3d.md)
takes a finished 2D ggplot and draws its panel, every layer with its
background and grid lines, on a plane of the box. The plot below shows z
against x with a linear fit, and it is placed on the back wall at the
largest y. It keeps its own coordinates, so its x and z line up with the
axes of the box.

``` r

side <- ggplot(cloud, aes(x, z)) +
  geom_point(colour = "#9E5E0F", size = 1) +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", formula = y ~ x, colour = "#2E6F9E")
k + annotation_plot_3d(side, plane = "xz", at = Inf) +
  geom_point_3d(size = 2.5) +
  coord_3d()
```

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The vector route places the panel’s marks in the wall plane, where they
are foreshortened with the box and covered by geometry in front. Text
faces the viewer and draws over the scene. The panel background and grid
travel with the panel; its outer axes, title and legend stay outside the
embedded panel.

The two letters of the plane name select the directions of the 2D plot’s
x and y axes. The remaining coordinate is fixed by the placement
argument. A four-value extent can position the plot independently of its
original ranges.

``` r

bars <- ggplot(mtcars, aes(factor(cyl))) + geom_bar(fill = "#2E6F9E")
k + annotation_plot_3d(bars, plane = "xy", at = -Inf,
                       extent = c(-2, 2, -2, 2), alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_point_3d(size = 2) + coord_3d()
```

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

For a dense panel, choose the raster route and set its image resolution.
The following example uses a small resolution to keep the article fast.
Both routes accept one 2D panel; place several panels with separate
calls.

``` r

k + annotation_plot_3d(side, plane = "xz", at = Inf,
                       backend = "raster", resolution = 64) +
  geom_point_3d(size = 2.5) + coord_3d()
```

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

See
[annotation_plot_3d()](https://gillescolling.com/ggplot3d/reference/annotation_plot_3d.md)
for all plane orientations and placement arguments.

## Small multiples in depth

[`facet_slices_3d()`](https://gillescolling.com/ggplot3d/reference/facet_slices_3d.md)
splits the data like
[`facet_wrap()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/facet_wrap.html)
and stacks the subsets on parallel planes of one panel. The cloud is
split by the sign of x; each half gets its own density, computed within
its slice.

``` r

cloud$side <- ifelse(cloud$x < 0, "negative", "positive")
ggplot(cloud, aes(z)) +
  geom_density(fill = "#2E6F9E", alpha = 0.6) +
  facet_slices_3d(vars(side), labels = FALSE) +
  coord_3d(up = "y", azimuth = 30, elevation = 20)
```

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The slices lie on z, so the 2D layers keep x and y; `coord_3d(up = "y")`
stands the planes upright, one behind the other. A numeric slicing
variable places slices at its values on a continuous scale. A factor
uses its level order, and layers without the slicing variable repeat in
every slice. Plane visibility, labels and opacity are set in
[facet_slices_3d()](https://gillescolling.com/ggplot3d/reference/facet_slices_3d.md).

## Reference lines and annotations

[`geom_hline()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/geom_abline.html)
and
[`geom_vline()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/geom_abline.html)
draw lines on the floor, here at x = 0 and y = 0.
[`annotate_3d()`](https://gillescolling.com/ggplot3d/reference/annotate_3d.md)
adds z positions to the arguments of
[`annotate()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/annotate.html).
Here it labels the highest point of the cloud. [Choosing layers for
observations and
grids](https://gillescolling.com/ggplot3d/articles/layers.html#reference-lines-and-dimensions)
shows arbitrary reference lines, brackets and dimension lines.

``` r

top <- cloud[which.max(cloud$z), ]
k + geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "#5C6166") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "#5C6166") +
  geom_point_3d(size = 2.5) +
  annotate_3d("label", x = top$x, y = top$y, z = top$z, label = "highest",
              hjust = -0.15) +
  coord_3d()
```

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The label is a box drawn at the projected position of its point, over
the whole scene, so points and faces in front of that position never
cover it.

## Contours and densities on the floor

The surface below has a peak and a hollow. `surface` contains one row
for each of 25 by 25 grid positions with the height `z`.

``` r

surface <- expand.grid(x = seq(-2, 2, length.out = 25),
                       y = seq(-2, 2, length.out = 25))
surface$z <- with(surface, exp(-((x - 0.5)^2 + y^2)) -
  0.6 * exp(-((x + 0.8)^2 + (y + 0.6)^2) / 0.5))
```

### Terraced filled contours

ggplot2’s own filled contour layer works with the z mapping. Each band
occupies a horizontal plane at the midpoint of its lower and upper
levels, and the ordered band factor uses a discrete fill scale. Holes
inside a band remain open.

``` r

ggplot(surface, aes(x, y, z = z)) +
  geom_contour_filled(bins = 5, colour = "white", linewidth = 0.15) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("#7A4F9E", "#2E6F9E", "#2A7A7A", "#3F7A3D", "#9E5E0F")) +
  coord_3d(elevation = 40)
```

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

### A contour map beneath a surface

[`geom_contour_filled_3d()`](https://gillescolling.com/ggplot3d/reference/geom_contour_3d.md)
with `plane = "floor"` computes height bands from the same grid and
draws them flat on the floor, giving a contour map under the surface. A
higher camera elevation shows more of the floor.

``` r

ramp <- c("#DCEAF3", "#2E6F9E")
s <- ggplot(surface, aes(x, y, z = z))
s + geom_contour_filled_3d(plane = "floor", bins = 6) +
  geom_surface_3d(fill = "grey85") +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = ramp[1], high = ramp[2]) +
  coord_3d(elevation = 40)
```

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The bands are computed in the same z units as the surface, so the
darkest band on the floor sits under the peak and the lightest under the
hollow.

A density surface can stand over the observations it was estimated from.
`faithful` records the duration and the waiting time of 272 eruptions of
the Old Faithful geyser.
[`stat_density_2d_3d()`](https://gillescolling.com/ggplot3d/reference/stat_density_2d_3d.md)
draws the estimated density, and the eruptions are drawn on the floor
with `z = -Inf`. The surface is half transparent and the camera is
raised, so the points under the two peaks show through. The z title is
set with [`labs()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/labs.html)
because the density layer computes z and has no z mapping to name it.

``` r

ggplot(faithful, aes(eruptions, waiting)) +
  stat_density_2d_3d(n = 24, alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_point_3d(aes(z = -Inf), size = 1) +
  labs(z = "density") +
  coord_3d(elevation = 50)
```

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

With `plane = "floor"`,
[`stat_density_2d_3d()`](https://gillescolling.com/ggplot3d/reference/stat_density_2d_3d.md)
lays the same density grid flat on the floor and fills it by density, a
heat map under the surface.

``` r

ggplot(faithful, aes(eruptions, waiting)) +
  stat_density_2d_3d(n = 24, alpha = 0.5) +
  stat_density_2d_3d(n = 48, plane = "floor") +
  labs(z = "density") +
  coord_3d(elevation = 50)
```

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

## A 3D panel beside 2D panels

A ggplot3d plot is a ggplot object, so patchwork arranges it with 2D
plots. The surface is coloured by height and stacked above a 2D raster
of the same grid. Both plots use the same fill scale, so
`guides = "collect"` draws one legend for both.

``` r

heights <- scale_fill_gradient2(low = "#B5342B", mid = "#F2F2F2",
  high = "#2E6F9E", limits = c(-0.6, 1), name = "z")
top <- s + stat_surface_3d(aes(fill = after_stat(z_mean))) +
  heights + coord_3d()
map <- ggplot(surface, aes(x, y, fill = z)) + geom_raster() +
  heights + coord_equal()
top / map + plot_layout(guides = "collect") &
  theme(legend.position = "right")
```

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The 3D panel colours each triangle by its mean height, and the raster
colours each grid cell by its height. The colours agree because the two
plots share the limits of `heights`.

A profile shows one line of the surface at full resolution. `profile`
contains the grid rows with y = 0. The same rows are drawn as a red path
on the 3D surface and as a 2D line against x.

``` r

profile <- surface[abs(surface$y) < 1e-9, ]
across <- s + geom_surface_3d(fill = "grey85") +
  geom_path_3d(data = profile, colour = "#B5342B", linewidth = 1) +
  coord_3d()
side <- ggplot(profile, aes(x, z)) +
  geom_line(colour = "#B5342B", linewidth = 1)
across / side
```

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

The x axis has the same range in both panels, so the hollow near x = -1
and the peak near x = 0.5 appear at the same x in the path and in the
profile.

## Two camera views of one plot

The camera arguments of
[`coord_3d()`](https://gillescolling.com/ggplot3d/reference/coord_3d.md)
take one value per panel. To show the same data from two directions,
repeat the data once per view, facet by the view, and give each panel
its own angles.

``` r

views <- rbind(transform(surface, view = "default view"),
               transform(surface, view = "from the opposite side"))
ggplot(views, aes(x, y, z = z)) + geom_surface_3d(fill = "grey85") +
  facet_wrap(~view, ncol = 1) +
  coord_3d(azimuth = c(-60, 120), elevation = c(30, 55))
```

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Both panels keep one magnification, so the surface has the same size in
each. Separate plots with their own
[`coord_3d()`](https://gillescolling.com/ggplot3d/reference/coord_3d.md),
arranged with patchwork, do the same for plots with different data.

``` r

base <- s + geom_surface_3d(fill = "grey85")
(base + coord_3d()) /
  (base + coord_3d(azimuth = 120, elevation = 55))
```

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

[Choosing camera
views](https://gillescolling.com/ggplot3d/articles/camera.md) describes
the angles. [Scaling heights and facet
ranges](https://gillescolling.com/ggplot3d/articles/z-scale.md) shows
facets with fixed and free z ranges.

## Titles and captions

Titles, subtitles and captions are drawn outside the panel in page
coordinates, as in any ggplot2 plot.

``` r

base + coord_3d() +
  labs(title = "Two Gaussian features",
       subtitle = "Peak near (0.5, 0), hollow near (-0.8, -0.6)",
       caption = "Heights on a 25 by 25 grid")
```

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

In a patchwork layout the same
[`labs()`](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/reference/labs.html) call names
one panel, and
[`plot_annotation()`](https://patchwork.data-imaginist.com/reference/plot_annotation.html)
adds a title over the whole arrangement.

``` r

across / side + plot_annotation(title = "Profile at y = 0")
```

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)
